claim: 80 subjects performed a continuous version of the random dot motion task.
source: 80 subjects performed a continuous version of the random dot motion task in which they were asked to report temporally and spatially unpredictable periods of coherent motion within either of two streams of random motion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Subjects were asked to report temporally and spatially unpredictable periods of coherent motion within either of two streams of random motion.
source: 80 subjects performed a continuous version of the random dot motion task in which they were asked to report temporally and spatially unpredictable periods of coherent motion within either of two streams of random motion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the task requirements for subjects.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter was computed as the average pupil diameter over the 100 ms preceding target onset.
source: Baseline pupil diameter was computed as the average pupil diameter over the 100 ms preceding target onset.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how baseline pupil diameter was measured.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter displayed a non-monotonic relationship with RT.
source: We found that baseline pupil diameter displayed a non-monotonic relationship with both measures of behavioural performance (RT χ2(1)=8.84, p=0.003; RTcv χ2(1)=4.43, p=0.035).
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter displayed a non-monotonic relationship with RTcv.
source: We found that baseline pupil diameter displayed a non-monotonic relationship with both measures of behavioural performance (RT χ2(1)=8.84, p=0.003; RTcv χ2(1)=4.43, p=0.035).
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: RT was slower on trials with higher baseline arousal levels.
source: Rather, RT was slower on trials with higher baseline arousal levels.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data analysis.

claim: The pupil diameter response displayed a non-monotonic relationship with RT.
source: The pupil diameter response, on the other hand, displayed a non-monotonic (but not U-shaped) relationship with RT (χ2(1)=51.89, p<0.001) and an inverse linear relationship with RTcv (χ2(1)=45.94, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: The pupil diameter response displayed an inverse linear relationship with RTcv.
source: The pupil diameter response, on the other hand, displayed a non-monotonic (but not U-shaped) relationship with RT (χ2(1)=51.89, p<0.001) and an inverse linear relationship with RTcv (χ2(1)=45.94, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: Best performance was found on trials with the largest pupil responses.
source: For both measures, best performance was found on trials with the largest pupil responses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data analysis and figure.

claim: The centro-parietal positivity (CPP) exhibits properties of accumulation of sensory evidence towards a decision bound.
source: The centro-parietal positivity (CPP) measured from scalp EEG exhibits many of these same properties, including a representation of the accumulation of sensory evidence towards a decision bound (O'Connell et al., 2012; O'Connell et al., 2018; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The onset latency of the CPP displayed an inverse monotonic relationship with the size of the pupil response.
source: We found that the onset latency of the CPP, defined as the first time point that showed a significant difference from zero for 15 consecutive time points, displayed an inverse monotonic relationship with the size of the pupil response (χ2(1)=5.60, p=0.018), such that the fastest onsets were found for the largest pupil response bins (Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical test results and figure reference support this relationship.

claim: The build-up rate of the CPP varied with the pupil response, displaying the steepest slope on trials with the largest pupil dilations.
source: Likewise, the build-up rate (χ2(1)=4.45, p=0.035), but not the amplitude (p=0.15), of the CPP varied with the pupil response, displaying the steepest slope on trials with the largest pupil dilations.
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: The amplitude of the CPP did not vary with the pupil response.
source: Likewise, the build-up rate (χ2(1)=4.45, p=0.035), but not the amplitude (p=0.15), of the CPP varied with the pupil response, displaying the steepest slope on trials with the largest pupil dilations.
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: There is an approximately linear relationship between pupil diameter response and the consistency of the CPP signal.
source: We found an approximately linear relationship between pupil diameter response and the consistency of the CPP signal (χ2(1)=41.79, p<0.001), indicating that the CPP signal is less variable for larger pupil response bins (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical test results and figure reference support this relationship.

claim: The CPP signal is less variable for larger pupil response bins.
source: We found an approximately linear relationship between pupil diameter response and the consistency of the CPP signal (χ2(1)=41.79, p<0.001), indicating that the CPP signal is less variable for larger pupil response bins (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the ITPC analysis results.

claim: Pre-target α-band power has been shown to vary with behavioural performance.
source: We next investigated pre-target preparatory α-band power (8–13 Hz), a sensitive index of attentional deployment that has been shown to vary with behavioural performance.
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in the literature.

claim: Previous studies have found higher pre-target α-band power preceding trials with longer RT.
source: Specifically, previous studies have found higher pre-target α-band power preceding trials with longer RT, and suggested that fluctuations in α-power may reflect an attentional influence on variability in task performance (Ergenoglu et al., 2004; van Dijk et al., 2008; O'Connell et al., 2009; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is an approximately linear relationship between α-band power and RT.
source: We replicated previous findings (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013) and found an approximately linear relationship between α-band power and RT (χ2(1)=25.27, p<0.001) but not RTcv (p=0.48).
evidence: Statistical test results support this relationship.

claim: There is no significant relationship between α-band power and RTcv.
source: We replicated previous findings (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013) and found an approximately linear relationship between α-band power and RT (χ2(1)=25.27, p<0.001) but not RTcv (p=0.48).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: Pupil diameter response was inversely related to α-band power.
source: In line with previous research (Hong et al., 2014), pupil diameter response was inversely related to α-band power (Figure 3B), displaying an approximately linear relationship (χ2(1)=28.24, p<0.001), suggesting that pre-target attentional engagement is related to phasic arousal.
evidence: Statistical test results, figure reference, and citation support this relationship.

claim: Pre-target attentional engagement is related to phasic arousal.
source: In line with previous research (Hong et al., 2014), pupil diameter response was inversely related to α-band power (Figure 3B), displaying an approximately linear relationship (χ2(1)=28.24, p<0.001), suggesting that pre-target attentional engagement is related to phasic arousal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between pupil response and α-band power.

claim: LHB decreases before a button press and has been shown to reflect the motor-output stage of perceptual decision making.
source: LHB decreases before a button press and has been shown to reflect the motor-output stage of perceptual decision making, but also to trace decision formation, reflecting the build-up of choice selective activity (Donner et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neither LHB amplitude nor LHB slope varied with phasic arousal.
source: We found that neither LHB amplitude (p=0.63) nor LHB slope (p=0.20) varied with phasic arousal, suggesting that phasic arousal does not influence the build-up rate of choice-related activity over motor cortex.
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationships.

claim: Phasic arousal does not influence the build-up rate of choice-related activity over motor cortex.
source: We found that neither LHB amplitude (p=0.63) nor LHB slope (p=0.20) varied with phasic arousal, suggesting that phasic arousal does not influence the build-up rate of choice-related activity over motor cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of significant relationships.

claim: The pupil response was not predictive of N2c latency.
source: Specifically, phasic arousal was not predictive of N2c latency (p=0.82) or amplitude (p=0.64), nor did we find any relationship between the pupil response and the N2c ITPC (p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: The pupil response was not predictive of N2c amplitude.
source: Specifically, phasic arousal was not predictive of N2c latency (p=0.82) or amplitude (p=0.64), nor did we find any relationship between the pupil response and the N2c ITPC (p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: There is no relationship between the pupil response and the N2c ITPC.
source: Specifically, phasic arousal was not predictive of N2c latency (p=0.82) or amplitude (p=0.64), nor did we find any relationship between the pupil response and the N2c ITPC (p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: The pupil response was not predictive of N2i latency.
source: Likewise, the pupil response was not predictive of N2i latency (p=0.64), amplitude (p=0.11) or ITPC (p=0.87).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: The pupil response was not predictive of N2i amplitude.
source: Likewise, the pupil response was not predictive of N2i latency (p=0.64), amplitude (p=0.11) or ITPC (p=0.87).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: The pupil response was not predictive of N2i ITPC.
source: Likewise, the pupil response was not predictive of N2i latency (p=0.64), amplitude (p=0.11) or ITPC (p=0.87).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: The addition of pre-target α-power significantly improved the model fit for predicting RT compared to the baseline model with pupil bin.
source: Compared to the baseline model predicting RT with pupil bin, the addition of pre-target α-power significantly improved the model fit (χ2(1)=10.30, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results support this improvement in model fit.

claim: The addition of CPP onset significantly improved the model fit for predicting RT.
source: We found that both the addition of CPP onset (χ2(1)=8.24, p=0.004) as well as the build-up rate (χ2(1)=4.90, p=0.027) significantly improved the model fit.
evidence: Statistical test results support this improvement in model fit.

claim: The addition of CPP build-up rate significantly improved the model fit for predicting RT.
source: We found that both the addition of CPP onset (χ2(1)=8.24, p=0.004) as well as the build-up rate (χ2(1)=4.90, p=0.027) significantly improved the model fit.
evidence: Statistical test results support this improvement in model fit.

claim: The addition of CPP amplitude did not improve the model fit for predicting RT.
source: Whereas the addition of CPP amplitude did not (χ2(1)=1.43, p=0.23), the addition of CPP ITPC substantially improved the fit of the model (χ2(1)=19.25, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant improvement in model fit.

claim: The addition of CPP ITPC substantially improved the fit of the model for predicting RT.
source: Whereas the addition of CPP amplitude did not (χ2(1)=1.43, p=0.23), the addition of CPP ITPC substantially improved the fit of the model (χ2(1)=19.25, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results support this substantial improvement in model fit.

claim: Neither the LHB build-up rate nor amplitude improved the fit of the model for predicting RT.
source: Neither the LHB build-up rate nor amplitude improved the fit of the model (LHB build-up rate χ2(1)=0.02, p=0.88; amplitude χ2(1)=0.64, p=0.42).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant improvements in model fit.

claim: Only pre-target α-power and CPP ITPC significantly improved the model fit for predicting RT after stepwise model selection.
source: This procedure eliminated CPP onset (F(1) = 0.06, p=0.80) and build-up rate (F(1) = 1.86, p=0.17) from the final model. Thus, only pre-target α-power and CPP ITPC significantly improved the model fit for predicting RT.
evidence: Statistical test results from stepwise model selection support this conclusion.

claim: The fixed effects of the final model (pre-target α-power and CPP ITPC) explained 15.8% of the variability in RT across the five pupil response bins.
source: The fixed effects of the model (the neural signals) explained 15.8% of the variability in RT (marginal r2) across the five pupil response bins, and together with the random effects (across subject variability) it explained 92.6% of the variability (conditional r2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the model's explanatory power.

claim: CPP ITPC was the only variable that exerted independent influence on RTcv.
source: The hierarchical regression analysis revealed that both CPP onset and CPP ITPC improved the model fit, but eliminated CPP onset after the forward/backward model selection. Consequently, CPP ITPC was the only variable that exerted independent influence on RTcv.
evidence: Statistical test results from hierarchical regression and model selection support this conclusion.

claim: CPP ITPC was the strongest predictor for RT.
source: From this analysis we can conclude that CPP ITPC was the strongest predictor for RT and the only predictor for RTcv.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hierarchical regression analysis results.

claim: CPP ITPC was the only predictor for RTcv.
source: From this analysis we can conclude that CPP ITPC was the strongest predictor for RT and the only predictor for RTcv.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hierarchical regression analysis results.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the CPP onset.
source: Unlike the pupil response, baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the onset (p=0.20) or build-up rate (p=0.12), but it displayed an inverse relationship with both the amplitude (χ2(1)=7.09, p=0.01) and the consistency of the CPP (χ2(1)=9.34, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the CPP build-up rate.
source: Unlike the pupil response, baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the onset (p=0.20) or build-up rate (p=0.12), but it displayed an inverse relationship with both the amplitude (χ2(1)=7.09, p=0.01) and the consistency of the CPP (χ2(1)=9.34, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter displayed an inverse relationship with CPP amplitude.
source: Unlike the pupil response, baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the onset (p=0.20) or build-up rate (p=0.12), but it displayed an inverse relationship with both the amplitude (χ2(1)=7.09, p=0.01) and the consistency of the CPP (χ2(1)=9.34, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test results support this inverse relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter displayed an inverse relationship with the consistency of the CPP.
source: Unlike the pupil response, baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the onset (p=0.20) or build-up rate (p=0.12), but it displayed an inverse relationship with both the amplitude (χ2(1)=7.09, p=0.01) and the consistency of the CPP (χ2(1)=9.34, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test results support this inverse relationship.

claim: Higher baseline pupil diameter displayed lower EEG signal consistency.
source: In line with previous research that revealed increased variability in the rate of evidence accumulation during periods with larger baseline pupil diameter (Murphy et al., 2014b), we found an inverse, approximately linear, relationship in which higher baseline pupil diameter displayed lower EEG signal consistency (Figure 4D).
evidence: This observation is supported by data analysis, figure reference, and citation to previous research.

claim: States of higher arousal are characterized by less consistency, that is more variability, in decision processing.
source: Thus, states of higher arousal are characterized by less consistency, that is more variability, in decision processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed inverse relationship between baseline pupil diameter and CPP consistency.

claim: Higher variability in decision processing (due to higher tonic arousal) can affect behavioural performance.
source: Additionally, states of higher tonic arousal also display lower task performance (Figure 1C), indicating that higher variability in decision processing (due to higher tonic arousal) can affect behavioural performance.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed relationships between baseline pupil diameter, CPP consistency, and task performance.

claim: Pre-target alpha power varied with baseline pupil diameter in a non-monotonic, but not inverted-U shaped, manner.
source: Specifically, as observed before (Hong et al., 2014), pre-target alpha power (Figure 5A) varied with baseline pupil diameter in a non-monotonic, but not inverted-U shaped, manner (χ2(1)=4.49, p=0.034).
evidence: Statistical test results, figure reference, and citation support this relationship.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between baseline pupil diameter and LHB build-up rate.
source: We found an inverse relationship with LHB build-up rate (χ2(1)=10.99, p<0.001), decreasing with larger baseline pupil diameter, but we did not find a relationship with LHB amplitude (p=0.34).
evidence: Statistical test results support this inverse relationship.

claim: There is no relationship between baseline pupil diameter and LHB amplitude.
source: We found an inverse relationship with LHB build-up rate (χ2(1)=10.99, p<0.001), decreasing with larger baseline pupil diameter, but we did not find a relationship with LHB amplitude (p=0.34).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the peak latency of the N2c.
source: Here we found that baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the peak latency of the N2c (p=0.75), but that it did display a monotonic relationship with the N2c amplitude (χ2(1)=13.72, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter displayed a monotonic relationship with the N2c amplitude.
source: Here we found that baseline pupil diameter was not predictive of the peak latency of the N2c (p=0.75), but that it did display a monotonic relationship with the N2c amplitude (χ2(1)=13.72, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test results support this monotonic relationship.

claim: Trials with larger baseline pupil diameter displayed smaller N2c amplitudes.
source: Trials with larger baseline pupil diameter displayed smaller N2c amplitudes, suggesting that higher arousal has a negative impact on sensory encoding.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data analysis.

claim: Higher arousal has a negative impact on sensory encoding.
source: Trials with larger baseline pupil diameter displayed smaller N2c amplitudes, suggesting that higher arousal has a negative impact on sensory encoding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between baseline pupil diameter and N2c amplitude.

claim: N2c ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter.
source: N2c ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter (p=0.25), and nor did N2i ITPC (p=0.33), N2i latency (p=0.78) or amplitude (p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: N2i ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter.
source: N2c ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter (p=0.25), and nor did N2i ITPC (p=0.33), N2i latency (p=0.78) or amplitude (p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: N2i latency did not vary with baseline pupil diameter.
source: N2c ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter (p=0.25), and nor did N2i ITPC (p=0.33), N2i latency (p=0.78) or amplitude (p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: N2i amplitude did not vary with baseline pupil diameter.
source: N2c ITPC did not vary with baseline pupil diameter (p=0.25), and nor did N2i ITPC (p=0.33), N2i latency (p=0.78) or amplitude (p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical test results indicate no significant relationship.

claim: N2c amplitude and CPP ITPC were the only parameters that were predictive of RT for tonic arousal after forward/backward model selection.
source: After the application of a forward/backward model selection algorithm (Venables and Ripley, 2002), N2c amplitude and CPP ITPC were the only parameters that were predictive of RT (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical model selection results support this conclusion.

claim: CPP ITPC was the only EEG component that explained unique variability in RTcv for tonic arousal.
source: This same hierarchical regression procedure revealed that CPP ITPC was the only EEG component that explained unique variability in RTcv (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical hierarchical regression results support this conclusion.

claim: The consistency of the CPP was the only stage of information processing that explained unique within and across-subject variability in task performance associated with changes in baseline pupil diameter.
source: Thus, additional to an effect of N2c amplitude on RT, the consistency of the CPP was the only stage of information processing that explained unique within and across-subject variability in task performance associated with changes in baseline pupil diameter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hierarchical regression analysis results.

claim: The trial-by-trial variability in both tonic and phasic arousal were predictive of behavioural performance.
source: We found that the trial-by-trial variability in both tonic and phasic arousal were predictive of behavioural performance (Figure 1B & C).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data analysis and figures.

claim: Both tonic and phasic arousal bore a predictive relationship with the neural signals coding for baseline attentional engagement, early target selection, decision processing as well as the preparatory motor response.
source: We furthermore established that both tonic and phasic arousal were predictive of a subset of EEG signatures, together reflecting discrete aspects of information processing underpinning perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by multiple data analyses.

claim: Unique variability in task performance due to tonic arousal could only be explained by the amplitude of target selection signals and the consistency of the CPP.
source: We found that pre-target α power, indexing baseline attentional engagement, and the consistency of the CPP, reflecting the decision formation, each explained unique variability in task performance that was due to variability in phasic arousal. Variability in task performance due to fluctuations in tonic arousal was explained by the amplitude of the target selection signal N2c and the consistency of the CPP.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the hierarchical regression analysis results.

claim: Variability in task performance due to phasic arousal was explained by pre-target α-band activity as well as the consistency of the CPP.
source: In contrast, variability due to phasic arousal (pupil response) was explained by pre-target α-band activity as well as the consistency of the CPP.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the hierarchical regression analysis results.

claim: Pupil diameter correlates strongly with a variety of measurements of cortical state and behavioural arousal.
source: Pupil diameter correlates strongly with a variety of measurements of cortical state and behavioural arousal (Eldar et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015b; McGinley et al., 2015a; Vinck et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016), and can thus be considered a reliable proxy of central arousal state.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is a strong correlation between pupil size and activity in various neuromodulatory centres that control arousal.
source: Indeed, there is a strong correlation between pupil size and activity in various neuromodulatory centres that control arousal (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2014a; Varazzani et al., 2015; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter correlates with sensory sensitivity.
source: Baseline pupil diameter correlates with sensory sensitivity (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b) and is predictive of behavioural performance during elementary detection tasks (Murphy et al., 2011; McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter is predictive of behavioural performance during elementary detection tasks.
source: Baseline pupil diameter correlates with sensory sensitivity (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b) and is predictive of behavioural performance during elementary detection tasks (Murphy et al., 2011; McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pupil diameter changes phasically in the course of a single decision.
source: Pupil diameter also changes phasically in the course of a single decision (Beatty, 1982a; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017; Lempert et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017), and has been related to specific elements of the decision making process, such as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017), uncertainty (Urai et al., 2017), and urgency (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Phasic pupil changes have been related to decision bias.
source: Pupil diameter also changes phasically in the course of a single decision (Beatty, 1982a; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017; Lempert et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017), and has been related to specific elements of the decision making process, such as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017), uncertainty (Urai et al., 2017), and urgency (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phasic pupil changes have been related to uncertainty.
source: Pupil diameter also changes phasically in the course of a single decision (Beatty, 1982a; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017; Lempert et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017), and has been related to specific elements of the decision making process, such as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017), uncertainty (Urai et al., 2017), and urgency (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phasic pupil changes have been related to urgency.
source: Pupil diameter also changes phasically in the course of a single decision (Beatty, 1982a; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017; Lempert et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017), and has been related to specific elements of the decision making process, such as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017), uncertainty (Urai et al., 2017), and urgency (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subjects performed at ceiling (mean, 98.7%; range: 92–100%).
source: As stimuli were presented well above perceptual threshold, our subjects performed at ceiling (mean, 98.7%; range: 92–100%, Newman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of task performance data with a citation.

claim: Reaction times were shorter on trials with lower tonic, and higher phasic arousal.
source: Reaction times were shorter on trials with lower tonic, and higher phasic arousal.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by data analysis in the results.

claim: Tonic and phasic arousal measures were predictive of a unique set of EEG signatures that together represent multiple information processing steps of decision-making.
source: Additionally, these two pupil measures were predictive of a unique set of EEG signatures that together represent multiple information processing steps of decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by multiple data analyses in the results.

claim: Behavioural variability associated with fluctuations in tonic and phasic arousal was mediated by its effects on the EEG markers of attentional engagement, sensory processing and the variability in decision processing.
source: Finally, behavioural variability associated with fluctuations in tonic and phasic arousal, indicative of neuromodulators acting on multiple timescales, was mediated by its effects on the EEG markers of attentional engagement, sensory processing and the variability in decision processing.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by hierarchical regression analyses in the results.

claim: The neuromodulatory systems that control central arousal state have both tonic and phasic firing patterns that are recruited on different timescales and support different functional roles.
source: These modulatory systems have both tonic and phasic firing patterns that are recruited on different timescales and support different functional roles (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Dayan and Yu, 2006; Parikh et al., 2007; Parikh and Sarter, 2008; Sarter et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Tonic changes in neuromodulator activity occur over longer timescales that can span multiple trials.
source: Tonic changes in neuromodulator activity occur over longer timescales that can span multiple trials, whereas fast (task-evoked) recruitment through phasic activation occurs on short enough timescales to influence neural activity and behavioural decisions within the same trial (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Dayan and Yu, 2006; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Fast (task-evoked) recruitment through phasic activation occurs on short enough timescales to influence neural activity and behavioural decisions within the same trial.
source: Tonic changes in neuromodulator activity occur over longer timescales that can span multiple trials, whereas fast (task-evoked) recruitment through phasic activation occurs on short enough timescales to influence neural activity and behavioural decisions within the same trial (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Dayan and Yu, 2006; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Data were collected under identical experimental procedures at either Monash University, Australia, or Trinity College Dublin, Ireland.
source: Data were collected under identical experimental procedures at either Monash University, Australia, or Trinity College Dublin, Ireland.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection procedures.

claim: A total of 288 trials were presented over 16 blocks (18 trials per block).
source: A total of 288 trials were presented over 16 blocks (18 trials per block).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The linear up-ramp model provided the best fit to the pupil data.
source: We found that the linear up-ramp model (model 3) provided the best fit to the data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model comparison results.

claim: Slow fluctuations in baseline pupil diameter (<0.01 Hz) are driving the effect on task performance.
source: This suggests that slow fluctuations in baseline pupil diameter (<0.01 Hz) are driving the effect on task performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of low-pass and band-pass filtered pupil data.

claim: There is no fixed delay between target selection and the response.
source: This indicates that there is no fixed delay between target selection and the response, and that there is variability in the duration of the sustained period of this task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of stimulus-locked and response-locked N2c signals.

claim: There is variability in the duration of the sustained period of this task.
source: This indicates that there is no fixed delay between target selection and the response, and that there is variability in the duration of the sustained period of this task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of stimulus-locked and response-locked N2c signals.

claim: Direct electrophysiological recordings from the LC have revealed a positive correlation between LC phasic activity and behavioural performance on elementary target detection tasks.
source: Direct electrophysiological recordings from the LC have revealed a positive correlation between LC phasic activity and behavioural performance on elementary target detection tasks (Aston-Jones et al., 1994; Aston-Jones et al., 1997; Rajkowski et al., 1994; Rajkowski et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Cue detection is enhanced on trials with a larger cholinergic response.
source: Likewise, cue detection is enhanced on trials with a larger cholinergic response (Parikh et al., 2007), and previous studies have found that large pupil responses were predictive of higher behavioural performance (Beatty, 1982b; but see Kristjansson et al., 2009), and decreased decision bias (de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Large pupil responses were predictive of higher behavioural performance.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Large pupil responses were predictive of decreased decision bias.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Poor performance upon pupil constrictions is in line with studies showing that sensory target detection is suboptimal when a transient LC or BF response is absent.
source: Additionally, poor performance upon pupil constrictions is in line with studies showing that sensory target detection is suboptimal when a transient LC or BF response is absent (Aston-Jones et al., 1994; Rajkowski et al., 1994; Parikh et al., 2007; Gritton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Naturally occurring pupillary constrictions are preceded by transient activity decreases in the LC.
source: Moreover, naturally occurring pupillary constrictions are preceded by transient activity decreases in the LC (Joshi et al., 2016), and are associated with increased synchronization of cortical activity, a signature of cortical down states, as well as suboptimal processing of visual stimuli (Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pupillary constrictions are associated with increased synchronization of cortical activity, a signature of cortical down states, as well as suboptimal processing of visual stimuli.
source: Moreover, naturally occurring pupillary constrictions are preceded by transient activity decreases in the LC (Joshi et al., 2016), and are associated with increased synchronization of cortical activity, a signature of cortical down states, as well as suboptimal processing of visual stimuli (Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fluctuations in α synchronization have previously been related to variation in both arousal and attentional deployment.
source: Fluctuations in α synchronization have previously been related to variation in both arousal and attentional deployment (Ergenoglu et al., 2004; van Dijk et al., 2008; O'Connell et al., 2009; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Newman et al., 2016), often interpreted as a neurophysiological correlate of cortical excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Membrane potential recordings from sensory and association areas are closely tracked by baseline pupil diameter during epochs of quiet wakefulness.
source: During epochs of quiet wakefulness, membrane potential fluctuations of neurons in visual, somatosensory and auditory cortex are closely tracked by baseline pupil diameter (Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Small pupil diameter is characterized by prominent low-frequency (2–10 Hz) and nearly absent high-frequency oscillations (30–80 Hz).
source: Small pupil diameter is characterized by prominent low-frequency (2–10 Hz) and nearly absent high-frequency oscillations (30–80 Hz), whereas larger pupil diameter is characterized by reduced low-frequency, but increased high-frequency oscillations (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Larger pupil diameter is characterized by reduced low-frequency, but increased high-frequency oscillations.
source: Small pupil diameter is characterized by prominent low-frequency (2–10 Hz) and nearly absent high-frequency oscillations (30–80 Hz), whereas larger pupil diameter is characterized by reduced low-frequency, but increased high-frequency oscillations (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The average subthreshold membrane potential is most stable during intermediate pupil diameter.
source: Thus, the average subthreshold membrane potential is most stable during intermediate pupil diameter, when neither low nor high-frequency components predominate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on oscillatory patterns at different pupil diameters.

claim: States of lower variability are characterized by more reliable sensory responses, higher spike rates, increased neural gain and better behavioural performance.
source: States of lower variability are furthermore characterized by more reliable sensory responses, higher spike rates, increased neural gain and better behavioural performance (Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: During auditory target detection, human subjects displayed the least variable RT at intermediate baseline pupil diameter.
source: During auditory target detection, human subjects displayed the least variable RT at intermediate baseline pupil diameter, as well as the highest amplitudes of the P3 component elicited by task-relevant stimuli (Murphy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Human subjects displayed the highest amplitudes of the P3 component elicited by task-relevant stimuli at intermediate baseline pupil diameter.
source: During auditory target detection, human subjects displayed the least variable RT at intermediate baseline pupil diameter, as well as the highest amplitudes of the P3 component elicited by task-relevant stimuli (Murphy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Modelling studies suggested that higher arousal is specifically predictive of more variability in evidence accumulation.
source: For tonic arousal, our findings are largely in line with modelling studies which suggested that higher arousal is specifically predictive of more variability in evidence accumulation (Murphy et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is some evidence that an increase in arousal can increase the ability of a distractor to disrupt performance on a Go/No-Go task in non-human primates.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence that an increase in arousal, as measured by pupil diameter, can increase the ability of a distractor to disrupt performance on a Go/No-Go task in non-human primates (Ebitz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At high arousal levels, it is more difficult to focus on the task at hand.
source: At high arousal levels, performance might thus be negatively affected when the task requires the successful suppression of distracting information, that is with higher arousal it is more difficult to focus on the task at hand (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A negative correlation was found between baseline pupil diameter and the size of the pupillary response.
source: As in previous studies (Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2011; de Gee et al., 2014), we found a negative correlation between baseline pupil diameter and the size of the pupillary response.
evidence: This observation is supported by data analysis and citations to previous research.

claim: During decision-making both tonic and phasic activity in the (network of) neuromodulatory centres that control central arousal can affect behaviour.
source: These results indicate that during decision-making both tonic and phasic activity in the (network of) neuromodulatory centres that control central arousal can affect behaviour during perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Fluctuations in central arousal, mediated by neuromodulatory brainstem centres, act on multiple timescales to influence task performance through its effects on attentional engagement, sensory processing as well as decision formation.
